📌 Multithreading & Multiprocessing in Python – Foundations¶

1️⃣ Overview¶

What This Lecture Covers¶

  • What is a Program
  • What is a Process
  • What is a Thread
  • Memory structure of a process
  • Difference between single-threaded and multi-threaded execution
  • Conceptual foundation before practical implementation

Why This Matters¶

In real-world systems:

  • Web servers handle thousands of users.
  • ML pipelines process massive datasets.
  • Applications must run efficiently.

To achieve performance and responsiveness, developers use:

  • Multithreading
  • Multiprocessing

These concepts form the backbone of efficient system design.

2️⃣ Core Concepts Explained Clearly¶

🔹 2.1 What is a Program?¶

Simple Explanation¶

A program is a set of instructions written in a programming language.

Technical Explanation¶

A program is a passive entity consisting of:

  • Source code
  • Compiled instructions
  • Executable files

It becomes active only when executed.

Intuition¶

Think of a program as a recipe. It only becomes useful when someone actually cooks.

🔹 2.2 What is a Process?¶

Simple Explanation¶

A process is a program that is currently running.

Technical Definition¶

A process is:

An instance of a program in execution.

Each process has:

  • Its own memory space
  • System resources
  • Process ID (PID)

🔹 Process Memory Structure¶

A process typically contains:

Component Purpose
Code Segment Executable instructions
Data Segment Global & static variables
Heap Dynamically allocated memory
Stack Local variables & function calls
Registers Temporary CPU storage

🔹 Key Property of Process¶

Each process has its own separate memory space.

This means:

  • One process cannot corrupt another process.
  • Fault isolation exists.
  • More secure execution.

🔹 Example¶

Opening multiple instances of:

  • Google Chrome
  • Excel
  • Notepad

Each is a separate process.

You can verify this in:

  • Task Manager (Windows)
  • Activity Monitor (Mac)

🔹 Disadvantage of Processes¶

Because memory is isolated:

  • Switching between processes is costly.
  • Context switching takes time.
  • Higher memory usage.

🔹 2.3 What is a Thread?¶

Simple Explanation¶

A thread is a smaller unit of execution inside a process.

Technical Definition¶

A thread is the smallest unit of CPU execution within a process.

🔹 Key Difference from Process¶

Feature Process Thread
Memory Separate Shared
Creation Cost High Low
Communication IPC required Easy (shared memory)
Isolation Strong Weak

🔹 Thread Memory Model¶

Each thread:

  • Has its own stack

  • Has its own registers

  • Shares:

    • Code segment
    • Data segment
    • Heap

🔹 Example Intuition¶

Imagine MS Paint:

  • Opening MS Paint → Process
  • Clicking “Draw Rectangle” → Thread
  • Clicking “Draw Circle” → Another Thread

Same process, different execution paths.

3️⃣ Single-Threaded vs Multi-Threaded Process¶

🔹 Single-Threaded Process¶

  • Only one execution path
  • Tasks run sequentially
  • Simpler
  • Slower for complex workloads
Process
 ├── Code (shared)
 ├── Data (shared)
 ├── Heap (shared)
 └── Thread 1
       ├── Stack
       └── Registers

🔹 Multi-Threaded Process¶

  • Multiple execution paths
  • Threads share memory
  • Faster for I/O-bound tasks
  • Requires synchronization
Process
 ├── Code (shared)
 ├── Data (shared)
 ├── Heap (shared)
 ├── Thread 1
 │     ├── Stack
 │     └── Registers
 └── Thread 2
       ├── Stack
       └── Registers

4️⃣ Important Definitions¶

  • Program – Passive code instructions
  • Process – Active execution instance
  • Thread – Unit of execution inside process
  • Stack – Stores function calls & local variables
  • Heap – Dynamic memory
  • Context Switching – CPU switching between tasks

5️⃣ Mathematical Perspective (CPU Execution Model)¶

If:

[ T_{total} = T_{compute} + T_{waiting} ]

Then:

  • For I/O-bound systems: Multithreading reduces waiting time.
  • For CPU-bound systems: Multiprocessing improves compute performance.

6️⃣ Execution Flow Comparison¶

🔹 Process Execution¶

  1. OS loads program
  2. Memory allocated
  3. Process ID assigned
  4. Code executed
  5. Resources released

🔹 Thread Execution¶

  1. Thread created inside process
  2. Shares memory
  3. Executes task
  4. Ends without killing process

7️⃣ Real-World Applications¶

🔹 Multithreading Used In¶

  • Web servers
  • GUI applications
  • File downloads
  • I/O operations

🔹 Multiprocessing Used In¶

  • ML model training
  • Parallel data processing
  • Scientific computing
  • CPU-heavy simulations

8️⃣ Interview & Exam Focus¶

🔹 Common Questions¶

  1. What is the difference between program and process?
  2. Why are processes more secure?
  3. Why are threads faster to create?
  4. What is context switching?
  5. What resources are shared between threads?
  6. What is the disadvantage of multithreading?

🔹 Concept Traps¶

  • Threads do NOT have separate heap.
  • Processes do NOT share memory by default.
  • More threads ≠ always better performance.
  • Multithreading in Python has GIL limitation.

9️⃣ Common Misconceptions¶

  • “Threads run on different CPUs automatically” ❌
  • “Processes are always slower” ❌
  • “Multithreading improves CPU-bound tasks in Python” ❌ (due to GIL)

🔟 Quick Revision Summary¶

  • Program = Code
  • Process = Running program
  • Thread = Execution path inside process
  • Processes have separate memory
  • Threads share memory
  • Process switching is expensive
  • Thread creation is lightweight

🧠 Memory Hooks¶

  • Program → Recipe
  • Process → Cooking
  • Thread → Multiple chefs in same kitchen
  • Separate kitchen = Process
  • Shared kitchen = Threads

📌 Multithreading in Python – Practical Implementation & Performance Analysis¶

1️⃣ Overview¶

What This Lecture Covers¶

  • When to use multithreading
  • I/O-bound vs CPU-bound tasks
  • Creating threads using threading module
  • Using start() and join()
  • Measuring execution time
  • Understanding concurrent execution behavior

Why This Matters¶

Efficient applications:

  • Reduce waiting time
  • Improve throughput
  • Handle multiple operations simultaneously

Multithreading is especially powerful for I/O-bound workloads.

2️⃣ When Should You Use Multithreading?¶

🔹 1. I/O-Bound Tasks (Primary Use Case)¶

Definition¶

Tasks that spend more time waiting for:

  • File reads/writes
  • Database queries
  • Network requests
  • API calls
  • Disk operations

Why Threads Help¶

While one thread is waiting for I/O, another thread can execute.

This improves resource utilization.

🔹 2. Concurrent Execution¶

When you want multiple independent tasks to run simultaneously to improve application responsiveness.

Example:

  • Downloading files
  • Serving multiple users
  • Processing multiple I/O requests

3️⃣ Baseline: Sequential Execution (Single Thread)¶

Code Example (Without Multithreading)¶

import time

def print_numbers():
    for i in range(5):
        print(f"Number: {i}")
        time.sleep(2)

def print_letters():
    for letter in "ABCDE":
        print(f"Letter: {letter}")
        time.sleep(2)

start_time = time.time()

print_numbers()
print_letters()

end_time = time.time()
print("Total Time:", end_time - start_time)

What Happens?¶

  • print_numbers() runs fully
  • Then print_letters() runs
  • Each iteration sleeps 2 seconds
  • Total time ≈ 20 seconds

Execution is strictly sequential.

4️⃣ Introducing Multithreading¶

Step 1: Import Threading¶

import threading
import time

Step 2: Define Same Functions (I/O Simulation)¶

We simulate I/O using time.sleep(2).

Step 3: Create Threads¶

t1 = threading.Thread(target=print_numbers)
t2 = threading.Thread(target=print_letters)

Each thread has:

  • Own stack
  • Own registers
  • Shared heap and data

Step 4: Start Threads¶

t1.start()
t2.start()

Now both functions run concurrently.

Step 5: Wait for Threads to Finish¶

t1.join()
t2.join()

join() ensures:

  • Main thread waits
  • Both threads complete execution

Final Code (Multithreaded Version)¶

import threading
import time

def print_numbers():
    for i in range(5):
        print(f"Number: {i}")
        time.sleep(2)

def print_letters():
    for letter in "ABCDE":
        print(f"Letter: {letter}")
        time.sleep(2)

start_time = time.time()

t1 = threading.Thread(target=print_numbers)
t2 = threading.Thread(target=print_letters)

t1.start()
t2.start()

t1.join()
t2.join()

end_time = time.time()
print("Total Time:", end_time - start_time)

5️⃣ What You Observe¶

Output becomes interleaved:

Number: 0
Letter: A
Number: 1
Letter: B
...

Total time ≈ 10 seconds (approximately half)

Why?

Because while one thread sleeps:

  • The other executes.

6️⃣ Technical Explanation¶

Thread Execution Flow¶

  1. Main thread starts.
  2. Two worker threads created.
  3. OS scheduler allocates CPU time.
  4. When one thread sleeps → CPU switches to other.
  5. After completion → join() merges back to main thread.

Important Concept: Concurrency vs Parallelism¶

Term Meaning
Concurrency Tasks make progress together
Parallelism Tasks execute literally at same time (multiple cores)

In Python:

  • Multithreading gives concurrency.
  • Due to GIL, true parallelism is limited for CPU-bound tasks.

7️⃣ Why Time Reduced?¶

Let:

  • Each function takes 10 seconds individually.
  • Sequential = 10 + 10 = 20 seconds.
  • Multithreaded ≈ 10 seconds.

Because sleep (I/O wait) releases CPU.

8️⃣ Important Methods in Threading¶

🔹 Thread Creation¶

threading.Thread(target=function_name)

🔹 Start Execution¶

thread.start()

🔹 Wait for Completion¶

thread.join()

Without join():

  • Program may terminate before threads finish.

9️⃣ Key Interview Concepts¶

🔹 Why is multithreading good for I/O-bound tasks?¶

Because threads release CPU while waiting.

🔹 Why not good for CPU-bound tasks in Python?¶

Because of:

Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)¶

  • Only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time.
  • Limits CPU-bound parallelism.

For CPU-bound tasks → Use multiprocessing.

🔹 What happens if join() is not used?¶

  • Main thread may exit early.
  • Threads may not complete.

🔟 Common Mistakes¶

  • Forgetting join()
  • Using multithreading for CPU-heavy tasks
  • Not protecting shared variables (race conditions)
  • Assuming threads always run in parallel

1️⃣1️⃣ Practical Real-World Use Cases¶

  • Web scraping
  • Download managers
  • API batching
  • Logging systems
  • File reading operations
  • Database requests

1️⃣2️⃣ Performance Insight¶

Let:

[ T_{total} = T_{compute} + T_{waiting} ]

Multithreading reduces:

[ T_{waiting} ]

But does not significantly reduce:

[ T_{compute} ]

🔟 Quick Revision Summary¶

  • Use threads for I/O-bound tasks.
  • Create thread using threading.Thread().
  • Start using .start().
  • Wait using .join().
  • Multithreading improves throughput.
  • Python GIL limits CPU-bound performance.

🧠 Memory Hook¶

Thread = Worker Sleep = Waiting for resource Multiple workers = Work continues even if one waits

I/O-bound → Threads CPU-bound → Processes

📌 Multiprocessing in Python (Practical + Conceptual Understanding)¶

1️⃣ Overview¶

This lecture explains:

  • What multiprocessing is
  • When to use multiprocessing
  • How to implement it in Python
  • Difference between multiprocessing and multithreading
  • Practical execution with timing comparison

Multiprocessing enables true parallel execution using multiple CPU cores.

2️⃣ Core Concept: What is Multiprocessing?¶

🔹 Simple Explanation¶

Multiprocessing allows a program to:

  • Create multiple independent processes
  • Execute them in parallel
  • Utilize multiple CPU cores

🔹 Technical Explanation¶

A process:

  • Has its own memory space
  • Has its own Python interpreter
  • Has its own GIL (Global Interpreter Lock)

Thus:

Multiple processes can execute simultaneously without being blocked by Python’s GIL.

🔹 Intuition¶

Think of:

  • Threads → Multiple workers inside one office (shared space)
  • Processes → Multiple offices working independently

Multiprocessing = Multiple offices running tasks at the same time.

3️⃣ When to Use Multiprocessing?¶

✅ 1. CPU-Bound Tasks¶

Tasks that require heavy computation:

  • Mathematical calculations
  • Data processing
  • Model training
  • Scientific simulations

These tasks heavily use CPU cycles.

✅ 2. Using Multiple CPU Cores¶

Modern CPUs have:

  • 2 cores
  • 4 cores
  • 8+ cores

Multiprocessing allows you to:

  • Run separate processes on different cores
  • Achieve real parallelism

4️⃣ Practical Implementation¶

🔹 Step 1: Import Required Libraries¶

import multiprocessing
import time

🔹 Step 2: Define CPU-Bound Functions¶

Square Function¶

def square_numbers():
    for i in range(5):
        time.sleep(1)
        print(f"Square: {i * i}")

Cube Function¶

def cube_numbers():
    for i in range(5):
        time.sleep(1.5)
        print(f"Cube: {i * i * i}")

🔹 Step 3: Create Entry Point (Mandatory)¶

if __name__ == "__main__":

Why Required?¶

On Windows:

  • Multiprocessing uses spawn
  • Script gets re-imported
  • Without this guard → Infinite process creation

🔹 Step 4: Full Multiprocessing Code¶

import multiprocessing
import time

def square_numbers():
    for i in range(5):
        time.sleep(1)
        print(f"Square: {i * i}")

def cube_numbers():
    for i in range(5):
        time.sleep(1.5)
        print(f"Cube: {i * i * i}")

if __name__ == "__main__":

    start = time.time()

    p1 = multiprocessing.Process(target=square_numbers)
    p2 = multiprocessing.Process(target=cube_numbers)

    p1.start()
    p2.start()

    p1.join()
    p2.join()

    end = time.time()

    print("Total Time:", end - start)

5️⃣ Code Execution Flow¶

Step-by-step:¶

  1. Create process objects
  2. Start process execution
  3. OS assigns resources
  4. Processes execute independently
  5. join() waits for completion
  6. Timer calculates total execution time

6️⃣ Sample Output (Approximate)¶

Square: 0
Cube: 0
Square: 1
Cube: 1
Square: 4
Cube: 8
Square: 9
Cube: 27
Square: 16
Cube: 64
Total Time: ~7 seconds

7️⃣ Why Faster?¶

If executed sequentially:

  • Square → 5 seconds
  • Cube → 7.5 seconds
  • Total ≈ 12.5 seconds

With multiprocessing:

  • Both run in parallel
  • Total ≈ 7–8 seconds

Parallel execution reduces total runtime.

8️⃣ Key Differences: Thread vs Process¶

Feature Thread Process
Memory Shared Separate
GIL Affected Yes No
CPU-bound Performance Poor Excellent
I/O-bound Performance Excellent Overhead
Creation Cost Low High

9️⃣ Memory Structure Comparison¶

🔹 Multithreading¶

  • Shared:

    • Code segment
    • Data segment
    • Heap

  • Separate:

    • Stack
    • Registers

🔹 Multiprocessing¶

Each process has:

  • Separate memory
  • Separate heap
  • Separate stack
  • Separate registers
  • Separate GIL

This isolation increases safety but uses more memory.

🔟 Common Mistakes¶

❌ Forgetting if __name__ == "__main__" ❌ Not calling join() ❌ Assuming processes share variables ❌ Creating too many processes ❌ Using multiprocessing for lightweight tasks

1️⃣1️⃣ Important Definitions¶

  • Process: Independent execution unit with separate memory
  • CPU-bound task: Task limited by processor speed
  • Parallelism: Simultaneous execution on multiple cores
  • GIL: Global Interpreter Lock restricting thread parallelism in CPython

1️⃣2️⃣ Interview-Focused Questions¶

  1. Why is multiprocessing better for CPU-heavy tasks?
  2. What is GIL and how does multiprocessing bypass it?
  3. Why do we need __main__ guard?
  4. Difference between parallelism and concurrency?
  5. Why is multiprocessing memory expensive?

1️⃣3️⃣ Quick 2-Minute Revision¶

  • Use multiprocessing for CPU-bound tasks
  • Each process has separate memory
  • Bypasses GIL
  • Use Process(target=...)
  • Use start()
  • Use join()
  • Always use if __name__ == "__main__"

🧠 Memory Hook¶

CPU Heavy → Separate Processes I/O Heavy → Threads

Threads = Shared kitchen Processes = Separate houses

📌 ThreadPoolExecutor & ProcessPoolExecutor (Advanced Multithreading & Multiprocessing)¶

1️⃣ Overview¶

In this lecture, we move from:

  • Manual thread/process creation to
  • Executor-based thread and process management

Using:

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, ProcessPoolExecutor

These are higher-level abstractions that:

  • Automatically manage thread/process creation
  • Handle pooling
  • Improve code readability
  • Reduce boilerplate
  • Provide better scalability

🔹 PART 1: ThreadPoolExecutor (Advanced Multithreading)¶

2️⃣ Why ThreadPoolExecutor?¶

Instead of manually doing:

t1 = threading.Thread(...)
t1.start()
t1.join()

We let Python manage:

  • Thread creation
  • Scheduling
  • Reuse of threads
  • Cleanup

This improves:

  • Code maintainability
  • Efficiency
  • Production-level design

3️⃣ Basic Example¶

Step 1: Import Libraries¶

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
import time

Step 2: Define Function¶

def print_number(number):
    time.sleep(1)
    return f"Number: {number}"

Step 3: Input Data¶

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

Step 4: Use ThreadPoolExecutor¶

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as executor:
    results = executor.map(print_number, numbers)

    for result in results:
        print(result)

🔎 What Happens Internally?¶

  • 3 worker threads created
  • Tasks distributed among them
  • When one thread finishes → it picks next task
  • Threads are reused (pooling)

⏱ Why Faster?¶

Even with:

time.sleep(1)

If 5 tasks:

  • Sequential → 5 seconds
  • 3 threads → ~2 seconds

Because:

3 tasks run → then remaining 2

🔹 Key Benefits¶

Feature ThreadPoolExecutor
Automatic thread management ✅
Resource reuse ✅
Cleaner code ✅
Scalable ✅

🔹 When to Use?¶

  • I/O-bound tasks
  • API calls
  • File reading
  • Network operations
  • Database queries

🔹 PART 2: ProcessPoolExecutor (Advanced Multiprocessing)¶

4️⃣ Why ProcessPoolExecutor?¶

Instead of manually:

p1 = multiprocessing.Process(...)
p1.start()
p1.join()

We use:

ProcessPoolExecutor

This:

  • Manages processes automatically
  • Uses multiple CPU cores
  • Bypasses GIL
  • Best for CPU-heavy tasks

5️⃣ Example: CPU-bound Square Function¶

Step 1: Import¶

from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
import time

Step 2: Function¶

def square(number):
    time.sleep(2)
    return number * number

Step 3: Input List¶

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

Step 4: Mandatory Main Guard¶

if __name__ == "__main__":

Step 5: Full Implementation¶

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as executor:
        results = executor.map(square, numbers)

        for result in results:
            print(result)

⚠ Why __main__ Is Required?¶

On Windows:

  • Uses "spawn"
  • Script re-imported
  • Without guard → infinite process creation

⏱ Execution Behavior¶

If:

  • 5 numbers
  • 2 seconds sleep
  • 3 processes

Total time ≈ 4 seconds (not 10 seconds)

Because tasks run in parallel on separate cores.

🔥 ThreadPoolExecutor vs ProcessPoolExecutor¶

Feature ThreadPoolExecutor ProcessPoolExecutor
Best for I/O-bound CPU-bound
GIL limitation Yes No
Memory usage Low High
True parallelism ❌ ✅
Overhead Low High

🧠 Internal Architecture Understanding¶

ThreadPoolExecutor¶

  • Shared memory
  • Shared heap
  • Separate stacks
  • Affected by GIL

ProcessPoolExecutor¶

  • Separate memory
  • Separate heap
  • Separate stacks
  • Independent GIL
  • True parallelism

🚨 Common Errors¶

  1. ❌ Forgetting if __name__ == "__main__"
  2. ❌ Using multiprocessing for lightweight tasks
  3. ❌ Creating too many workers
  4. ❌ Assuming shared variables between processes
  5. ❌ Not understanding CPU-bound vs I/O-bound difference

  • ThreadPoolExecutor → I/O tasks
  • ProcessPoolExecutor → CPU tasks
  • Executor handles lifecycle automatically
  • Always use main guard for process pool
  • Pools reuse workers → efficient

Think of:

ThreadPool → Multiple clerks sharing same office ProcessPool → Multiple independent factories

Heavy computation → Factories Network waiting → Clerks

📌 Multithreading for I/O-Bound Tasks – Real-World Use Case: Web Scraping¶

1️⃣ Overview¶

In this lecture, we implement multithreading for a real-world scenario:

Fetching multiple web pages concurrently using threads.

Why?¶

Web scraping is an I/O-bound task because:

  • It waits for network responses
  • Most time is spent waiting for server replies
  • CPU usage is low during waiting time

Therefore:

Multithreading significantly improves performance.

2️⃣ Problem Statement¶

We want to fetch content from the following URLs:

  1. https://python.langchain.com/v0.2/docs/introduction/
  2. https://python.langchain.com/v0.2/docs/concepts/
  3. https://python.langchain.com/v0.2/docs/tutorials/

Goal:

  • Fetch HTML content
  • Extract text
  • Count total characters
  • Do this concurrently using threads

3️⃣ Why Multithreading Works Here¶

🔹 Without Threads¶

  • Fetch URL 1 → wait
  • Fetch URL 2 → wait
  • Fetch URL 3 → wait
  • Total time = Sum of all waiting times

🔹 With Threads¶

  • Start all requests simultaneously
  • While one waits → others execute
  • Total time ≈ Slowest request time

🔹 Implementation (Improved + Clean Version)¶

Step 1: Install Required Libraries¶

pip install requests beautifulsoup4

Step 2: Import Libraries¶

import threading
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

Step 3: Define URLs¶

urls = [
    "https://python.langchain.com/v0.2/docs/introduction/",
    "https://python.langchain.com/v0.2/docs/concepts/",
    "https://python.langchain.com/v0.2/docs/tutorials/"
]

Step 4: Define Scraping Function¶

def fetch_content(url):
    response = requests.get(url)
    soup = BeautifulSoup(response.content, "html.parser")

    text_length = len(soup.text)

    print(f"Fetched {text_length} characters from {url}")

Step 5: Create and Start Threads¶

threads = []

for url in urls:
    thread = threading.Thread(target=fetch_content, args=(url,))
    threads.append(thread)
    thread.start()

Step 6: Wait for All Threads to Complete¶

for thread in threads:
    thread.join()

print("All web pages fetched.")

🔹 Expected Output (Sample)¶

Fetched 7477 characters from introduction
Fetched 8986 characters from concepts
Fetched 6600 characters from tutorials
All web pages fetched.

Order may vary because threads execute concurrently.

🔥 Execution Flow¶

  1. Main thread creates worker threads

  2. Each thread:

    • Sends HTTP request
    • Waits for response
    • Parses HTML
    • Counts characters

  3. All threads run concurrently

  4. Main thread waits using join()

🔹 Why This Is Faster¶

Because:

  • Network waiting time overlaps
  • CPU is not blocked
  • Threads share memory
  • Low overhead compared to processes

🔥 Important Technical Insight¶

Threads Share:¶

  • Code segment
  • Data segment
  • Heap

Each thread has:

  • Separate stack
  • Separate registers

Perfect for I/O tasks.

🚨 Production-Level Improvements (Intermediate+)¶

In real-world scraping:

1️⃣ Add Exception Handling¶

def fetch_content(url):
    try:
        response = requests.get(url, timeout=5)
        response.raise_for_status()

        soup = BeautifulSoup(response.content, "html.parser")
        print(f"Fetched {len(soup.text)} characters from {url}")

    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error fetching {url}: {e}")

2️⃣ Use ThreadPoolExecutor (Cleaner Version)¶

Instead of manual thread creation:

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as executor:
    executor.map(fetch_content, urls)

Cleaner. More scalable. Production-ready.

🧠 Why Not Multiprocessing Here?¶

Multiprocessing is best for:

  • Heavy computation
  • Image processing
  • ML training
  • Data transformations

Web scraping is:

  • Network bound
  • Waiting-heavy

Thus:

Threads are better.

📌 Multithreading for Web Scraping – Intermediate Level (Production-Oriented)¶

Now we move beyond basic threading and implement a clean, scalable, and safer web scraping system using multithreading.

This level focuses on:

  • ThreadPoolExecutor
  • Proper error handling
  • Timeout management
  • Performance measurement
  • Clean architecture
  • Real-world improvements

1️⃣ Why Improve the Basic Version?¶

Your previous version:

  • Manually created threads
  • No timeout handling
  • No retry logic
  • No structured result collection

In production:

We must handle failures, delays, and scalability.

2️⃣ Improved Architecture (Intermediate Level)¶

We will:

  • Use ThreadPoolExecutor
  • Add timeout
  • Add exception handling
  • Measure total execution time
  • Return structured results

3️⃣ Clean Intermediate Implementation¶

Step 1: Import Required Libraries¶

import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
import time

Step 2: URL List¶

urls = [
    "https://python.langchain.com/v0.2/docs/introduction/",
    "https://python.langchain.com/v0.2/docs/concepts/",
    "https://python.langchain.com/v0.2/docs/tutorials/"
]

Step 3: Scraping Function (Improved)¶

def fetch_content(url):
    try:
        response = requests.get(url, timeout=5)
        response.raise_for_status()

        soup = BeautifulSoup(response.content, "html.parser")
        text_length = len(soup.text)

        return {
            "url": url,
            "characters": text_length,
            "status": "success"
        }

    except Exception as e:
        return {
            "url": url,
            "characters": 0,
            "status": f"error: {str(e)}"
        }

Step 4: ThreadPoolExecutor with Controlled Workers¶

if __name__ == "__main__":

    start = time.time()

    results = []

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as executor:
        futures = [executor.submit(fetch_content, url) for url in urls]

        for future in as_completed(futures):
            results.append(future.result())

    end = time.time()

Step 5: Print Structured Results¶

    for result in results:
        print(result)

    print(f"\nTotal Execution Time: {end - start:.2f} seconds")

4️⃣ Why This Version is Better¶

🔹 ThreadPoolExecutor¶

  • Automatically manages threads
  • Reuses threads
  • Cleaner syntax

🔹 Timeout Handling¶

timeout=5

Prevents hanging forever if server does not respond.

🔹 Error Handling¶

response.raise_for_status()

Handles:

  • 404 errors
  • 500 errors
  • Network failures

🔹 as_completed()¶

Instead of waiting sequentially:

  • Returns results as soon as each finishes
  • More efficient

5️⃣ Performance Comparison¶

Execution Type Approx Time
Sequential 6–8 seconds
Multithreaded 2–3 seconds

Because:

  • All requests happen simultaneously
  • Waiting overlaps

6️⃣ Understanding Thread Lifecycle¶

  1. Executor creates 3 worker threads

  2. Tasks assigned to workers

  3. Workers perform:

    • HTTP request
    • Parse HTML
    • Return result

  4. as_completed() yields results

  5. Executor shuts down automatically

7️⃣ Memory Behavior¶

Threads:

  • Share memory
  • Lightweight
  • Low creation cost

Perfect for:

  • Network I/O
  • File reading
  • Database queries

Because:

📌 Multiprocessing for CPU-Bound Tasks – Factorial Computation (Intermediate Level)¶

1️⃣ Overview¶

In this example, we implement multiprocessing for a real-world CPU-heavy task:

Computing factorials of large numbers in parallel.

Why Factorial?¶

  • Factorial grows extremely fast
  • Large inputs (e.g., 6000, 7000, 8000)
  • Requires heavy CPU computation
  • Perfect example of CPU-bound workload

2️⃣ Why Multiprocessing Here?¶

Without Multiprocessing:¶

  • Single core computes factorial sequentially
  • Other CPU cores remain idle
  • Slow performance

With Multiprocessing:¶

  • Work distributed across multiple cores
  • True parallel execution
  • Reduced total computation time

3️⃣ Important Setup: Large Integer Handling¶

Python limits large integer-to-string conversions.

So we use:

import sys
sys.set_int_max_str_digits(100000)

Why?¶

Factorial of 8000 has thousands of digits.

Without increasing this limit → Python throws a safety error.

4️⃣ Clean & Structured Implementation¶

Step 1: Import Libraries¶

import multiprocessing
import math
import time
import sys

Step 2: Allow Large Integer Handling¶

sys.set_int_max_str_digits(100000)

Step 3: Define Factorial Function¶

def compute_factorial(number):
    print(f"Computing factorial of {number}")
    
    result = math.factorial(number)
    
    return result

Step 4: Main Entry Point (Mandatory)¶

if __name__ == "__main__":

Why mandatory?

  • Windows uses spawn
  • Script re-imported
  • Prevents infinite process creation

Step 5: Input Large Numbers¶

numbers = [5000, 6000, 7000, 8000]

Step 6: Start Timer¶

start_time = time.time()

Step 7: Create Process Pool¶

with multiprocessing.Pool() as pool:
    results = pool.map(compute_factorial, numbers)

Step 8: End Timer¶

end_time = time.time()

Step 9: Print Time Taken¶

print(f"Time Taken: {end_time - start_time:.4f} seconds")

5️⃣ What Happens Internally?¶

🔹 Pool() Does:¶

  • Detect number of CPU cores
  • Create that many worker processes
  • Distribute numbers across cores
  • Run factorial computations in parallel

6️⃣ Why Is This Fast?¶

If your CPU has:

  • 8 cores
  • 16 cores
  • 32 cores

Then:

Each factorial runs on a separate core.

Total time ≈ Time of slowest factorial

Instead of:

Sum of all factorial times

7️⃣ Performance Insight¶

If sequential:

Mode Execution
Single process Slow
Multiprocessing Fast

Multiprocessing uses:

  • Separate memory
  • Separate GIL
  • True parallelism

8️⃣ Key Concept: CPU-Bound vs I/O-Bound¶

Task Type Use
Network calls Threading
File reading Threading
Heavy math Multiprocessing
ML training Multiprocessing

9️⃣ Why Pool is Better Than Manual Process Creation?¶

Instead of:

p1 = Process(...)
p2 = Process(...)

Pool:

  • Automatically manages processes
  • Reuses worker processes
  • Balances workload
  • Cleaner syntax

🔟 Important Interview Concepts¶

Q1: Why is factorial CPU-bound?¶

Because:

  • Continuous arithmetic computation
  • No waiting involved
  • Heavy processor usage

Q2: Why multiprocessing is better than threading here?¶

Because:

  • GIL blocks threads for CPU tasks
  • Processes have separate GIL
  • True parallelism achieved

Q3: What happens if numbers are extremely large (e.g., 50000)?¶

  • High memory usage
  • Potential system slowdown
  • Heavy CPU spike

1️⃣1️⃣ Common Mistakes¶

❌ Forgetting __main__ guard ❌ Using threading for CPU-heavy work ❌ Printing extremely large factorial results ❌ Creating too many processes

1️⃣2️⃣ Advanced Insight (Intermediate+)¶

Default Behavior of Pool()¶

If you don’t specify:

Pool()

It automatically uses:

Number of CPU cores

You can manually control:

Pool(processes=4)

🧠 Memory Hook¶

Heavy Math = Multiple Cores Waiting Network = Threads

Factorial = CPU Web Scraping = I/O

🔥 LEVEL 1 — Intermediate+¶

📌 Pool vs ProcessPoolExecutor¶

Both create process pools, but they differ in abstraction and flexibility.

1️⃣ multiprocessing.Pool¶

Traditional API¶

with multiprocessing.Pool(processes=4) as pool:
    results = pool.map(compute_factorial, numbers)

Characteristics¶

  • Older API
  • Simple
  • Blocks until complete
  • Less flexible for async handling

2️⃣ ProcessPoolExecutor (Modern)¶

from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as executor:
    results = executor.map(compute_factorial, numbers)

Advantages¶

  • Cleaner
  • Supports submit()
  • Supports as_completed()
  • Better error handling
  • Future objects

🔥 Key Difference¶

Feature Pool ProcessPoolExecutor
Modern API ❌ ✅
Futures support ❌ ✅
Better exception handling ❌ ✅
Production-friendly Medium High

🔥 LEVEL 2 — Advanced¶

Now we go deeper.

📌 map() vs apply() vs starmap()¶

1️⃣ map()¶

Parallel mapping for iterable:

pool.map(func, iterable)
  • Blocks
  • Returns ordered results

2️⃣ apply()¶

Executes single function:

pool.apply(func, args=(value,))
  • Blocks
  • Runs once
  • Not parallel mapping

3️⃣ starmap()¶

For multiple arguments:

def power(x, y):
    return x ** y

pool.starmap(power, [(2,3), (3,4)])

Useful when function takes multiple parameters.

📌 submit() + Future Objects (Advanced Pattern)¶

Using ProcessPoolExecutor:

from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor, as_completed

with ProcessPoolExecutor() as executor:
    futures = [executor.submit(compute_factorial, n) for n in numbers]

    for future in as_completed(futures):
        print(future.result())

Why Powerful?¶

  • Non-blocking
  • Results as soon as finished
  • Advanced error tracking
  • Timeout support

📌 Chunk Size Optimization (Performance Tuning)¶

By default:

  • Pool divides work automatically

But you can optimize:

pool.map(func, iterable, chunksize=2)

Why important?¶

If:

  • Too small chunks → Too much scheduling overhead
  • Too large chunks → Poor load balancing

Rule of thumb:

chunksize = len(iterable) // (number_of_processes * 4)

🔥 LEVEL 3 — System-Level Optimization¶

Now we move to architecture-level thinking.

📌 Understanding CPU Core Utilization¶

You can check:

import multiprocessing
print(multiprocessing.cpu_count())

If:

  • 8 cores
  • You create 16 processes

What happens?

  • Context switching overhead
  • CPU thrashing
  • Reduced performance

📌 Overhead of Process Creation¶

Process creation cost includes:

  • Memory allocation
  • Separate interpreter
  • Separate heap
  • IPC setup

Therefore:

Don’t create processes inside loops.

Wrong ❌

for n in numbers:
    p = Process(...)

Correct ✅

Use Pool.

📌 Inter-Process Communication (IPC)¶

Processes don’t share memory.

To share data:

  • Queue
  • Pipe
  • Manager
  • SharedMemory (advanced)

Example:

from multiprocessing import Manager

manager = Manager()
shared_list = manager.list()

📌 Memory Explosion Risk¶

Factorial(8000) generates thousands of digits.

If you:

  • Store 1000 such results
  • Keep them in RAM

You can crash system.

Solution:

  • Stream results
  • Write to disk
  • Avoid printing huge outputs

📌 When Multiprocessing Fails¶

It fails when:

  • Task is I/O bound
  • Data transfer between processes is large
  • CPU cores are saturated
  • Memory becomes bottleneck

📌 Amdahl’s Law (System Optimization Concept)¶

Maximum speedup:

[ Speedup = \frac{1}{(1 - P) + \frac{P}{N}} ]

Where:

  • P = parallel portion
  • N = number of cores

Even with 32 cores:

You don’t get 32x speedup.

Because:

Some parts are always sequential.

📌 Real-World Optimization Strategy¶

For ML engineers:

  • Use multiprocessing for preprocessing
  • Use GPU for training
  • Avoid unnecessary IPC
  • Use chunk batching
  • Profile before optimizing

📌 Production-Level Pattern¶

Hybrid Approach¶

  • Threading for I/O
  • Multiprocessing for CPU
  • Async for large-scale I/O
  • Distributed systems for massive scaling

🧠 Ultimate Mental Model¶

Threads: Lightweight Shared memory I/O efficient

Processes: Heavyweight Separate memory CPU efficient

Distributed: Multiple machines Massive scale
